excerpt: Finding a 1909 postcard tucked between forgotten pages led to an unexpected discovery: an oak tree that has managed to outlast a century of weather, change, and human appetite.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
The afternoon carried the still, deliberate character of a Saturday spent among dusty paper. I came home carrying a heavy canvas bag filled with second-hand books from the annual sale down at the local library—the sort of volumes that smell faintly of damp cellars and forgotten attics. As I sat at the table turning through the leaves of a thick text, something slipped from between the pages and fell softly to the floor.

It was a postcard, sepia-toned and worn at the edges, bearing a postmark from the autumn of 1909. On its face was a photograph of a magnificent oak tree, its vast limbs spreading out like the rafters of a barn, with half a dozen men perched along its branches like roosting birds. Looking at the frail 1-cent stamp, it was hard not to think about time and the slow decay that eventually claims men, trees, and postcards alike. Surely, I thought, that old giant had gone back into the soil long ago.

Nature, however, operates on its own schedule. Some months later, by a happy stroke of chance, I happened across a photo of that very same spot. There stood the oak—thicker in the trunk, perhaps, but undeniably the same tree, still holding its ground against a hundred winters.

A discovery like that lays a hold on a person. Driven by a simple desire to stand near something that had outlasted so much history, I set out one clear morning to find the exact spot where it grew.

When you stand beneath a tree of that size, you feel small in a very pleasant, grounding way. It rises into the air like a cathedral spire, rooted firmly in the dirt yet reaching constantly upward. It put me in mind of the old, patient forests Tolkien wrote about—places where the world seems older, larger, and far less hurried than daily life allows.

If gravity were not so insistent, you could almost believe those upper branches were reaching out to brush the bottom of the sky. Sitting there under its broad shadow, listening to the wind stir through the leaves, it was easy to imagine that the breeze was carrying off the small, unwritten prayers of everyone who had ever rested beneath it.

It has been ages now, and I wonder if the oak tree continues to defy gravity and the elements—not to mention human greed for more real estate. I was fortunate to have experienced such beauty and endurance, knowing that no postcard could ever do justice to such a blessing.
